state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let me ask you this: what would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, okay... so like, if I had simpler numbers, maybe 10 and 20? So the range would be 10. Then if I cut them in half I'd get 5 and 10, and the range would still be 5... wait, that changed though, didn't it? But if I add 3 to both of them I'd get 13 and 23, and that's still a range of 10... so actually maybe both of them could be right? I'm confused now.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It seems like you're starting to see how changing all values by the same proportion can affect the range differently. Can you think of another way to test this idea with different numbers?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the proportional change misconception through well-calibrated prompts that lead the student to discover the error independently, resulting in clear conceptual progress from believing only Tom is right to recognizing that Katie (not Tom) is correct.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide discovery, never directly reveals the answer, and successfully helps the student recognize their flawed reasoning through guided exploration with simpler examples.
